hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.
hero.alt: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.

slides.title: Re-read what you wrote in Lesson 1
slides.subtitle: Work alone and in silence. Do not change anything yet.

blocks.text: A drawing of a Kenyan kitchen with a jiko, a sufuria, a mwiko, a chopping board with onions and a recipe book on a shelf.
items: ugali_kitchen

A friendly flat cartoon of a Kenyan home kitchen: a charcoal jiko with a sufuria on top, a wooden mwiko, a chopping board with sliced onions, an open wooden door, and a shelf holding a closed recipe book with a pot picture on its cover.

blocks.text: A student in Nairobi cuts their finger slicing onions. Bleeding slows. A clot forms. The wound heals. How — cell by cell?

do: Before class: make sure every learner has their Lesson 1 diagram and written prediction (from teacher files or portfolios).
Write the phenomenon on the board in full before learners come in.
Tell learners to read their Lesson 1 diagram and ideas, and not to change anything.
Start the 4-minute timer.
Do not prompt or hint while learners read.
say: In Lesson 1, I asked you to explain what happens when you cut your finger. You made your best guess.
Today that same question is back. But this time you have eleven lessons of evidence behind you.
Before we talk, take 4 minutes in silence to re-read what you wrote in Lesson 1.
notes.wait_time: The full 4 minutes of silence. Do not prompt or hint.
look_for: Every learner has a Lesson 1 page in front of them. Check the whole room.
Learners are reading, not talking or writing yet.
if_then: If a learner cannot find their Lesson 1 page, say: 'Look through your notebook for the page about the cut finger. If it is missing, write what you remember thinking at the start.'
If learners start to talk, say: 'This part is private. Read your own ideas.'
notes.why_this_works: Going back to their own first ideas before any new input wakes up prior knowledge and shows who still holds misconceptions. The gap between then and now is what makes the class explanation feel earned. Common misconception: 'cells just heal the wound' as one process.

slides.title: What would you change today, and why?
slides.subtitle: Still private. Do not share yet.

items: memo :: Use a sticky note or write in a new colour
question :: What would you change, and why?
lightbulb :: Which new word or idea would you use now?

blocks.text: Do not change your Lesson 1 writing. Add to it.

do: Give the instruction, then start the 3-minute timer.
Learners work alone. They write on a sticky note or in a different colour pen.
Circulate quietly and read over shoulders.
Note 2–3 learners with the biggest shift in thinking. Cold-call them first in the Observe phase.
Note 1–2 learners with only partial understanding. Plan simple, targeted questions for them.
say: Without changing what you wrote, put a sticky note or write in a new colour: what would you change, and what new word or idea would you now use?
You have 3 more minutes.
look_for: Read at least 8–10 sticky notes as you circulate.
Strong sign: learners name specific cells (platelets, neutrophils, fibroblasts, epidermal cells) or organelles (nucleus, cell membrane, lysosomes) that were not in their Lesson 1 writing.
Red flag: a note says only 'cells heal the wound' with no detail. This learner needs targeted cold-calling and support in the Observe phase.
if_then: If a note says only 'cells heal the wound', crouch down and say quietly: 'Which cell? What does it look like? What is its job?' Then plan an easier question for this learner in the round.
If a learner says 'I have nothing to change', say: 'Look at the word wall. Which word could you add to your Lesson 1 idea?'
notes.why_this_works: Writing in a new colour makes the change visible to the learner and to you. Keeping it private lets every learner be honest before the class story begins.
answer_key: Model sticky note: 'I would change: in Lesson 1 I wrote that cells just fix the cut. Now I would say platelets form a clot, neutrophils engulf bacteria and fibroblasts make collagen, because each cell has its own shape and organelles for its job.'

slides.title: The class story: six stages
slides.subtitle: Listen, nod, add or challenge.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes to set up the round

items: scissors :: 1. Cut occurs
droplet :: 2. Bleeding begins
bandage :: 3. Clot forms
microbe :: 4. Immune response
arrows_cycle :: 5. Tissue rebuilding
check :: 6. Skin closes

blocks.text: Your ONE claim: which cell, its shape, its organelle, its job.

do: Draw a simple timeline on the board with the 6 stages: (1) Cut occurs, (2) Bleeding begins, (3) Bleeding slows and clot forms, (4) Immune response, (5) Tissue rebuilding, (6) Skin closes.
Choose 8 learners by name before you start. Do not use volunteers.
Put the learners with the strongest shift first. Give simpler questions to learners with partial understanding.
Keep a tick list of who has been called.
say: We are going to build the complete explanation together, out loud, in order, using everything we know.
I will call on students. When I call your name, give me ONE cell claim: which cell acts at that stage, what its shape is, what its key organelle or feature is, and what job it does.
One claim. Precise. Based on evidence. Everyone else, listen. If you agree, nod. If you would add or challenge, raise your hand.
look_for: Learners understand the rule: one claim per person, then everyone else listens and responds.
Learners are looking at the timeline, ready to follow.
if_then: If learners seem unsure, say: 'Point to the stage on the board. Then tell me the cell, its shape, its organelle and its job.'
notes.why_this_works: A clear routine tells every learner what a good answer sounds like and keeps the others thinking even when they are not called. This round is a public knowledge-building exercise, not a quiz.

slides.title: Stages 1 to 3: the cut and the clot
slides.subtitle: Cold-call: one claim each. Everyone else listens.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each of the 3 students

items: First cell to respond: what is its shape, and why does the shape matter?
Platelets: what is unusual about their structure? How does it help?
Which protein do platelets help deploy? Which organelle makes proteins?

do: Call Student A for question 1 (stages 1–2). Then Student B for question 2 and Student C for question 3 (both stage 3).
After each answer, rephrase it and write the key claim on the board at the correct stage.
If an answer is incomplete, open it to the class by asking for the organelle or structure detail.
Tick each learner as called.
say: [Name], what is the FIRST cell to respond when the cut happens? Describe its shape and why that shape matters.
[Name], platelets. What is unusual about platelet structure, and how does that unusual feature help them do their job?
[Name], what protein do platelets help deploy? What organelle in other cells produces proteins like that?
[Name], you said [X]. Can anyone add the organelle or structure detail that makes that work?
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after question 1, 12 seconds after question 2, 10 seconds after question 3.
look_for: Each called learner names the cell type and one structural feature without prompting. Target: 6 out of the 8 learners in the whole round do this.
Uncalled learners are nodding, following the board or raising hands to add.
If fewer than 4 learners can name the right organelle for a function, stop and run a 2-minute whole-class review of that organelle.
if_then: If an answer is incomplete, say: '[Name], you said [X]. Can anyone add the organelle or structure detail that makes that work?'
If a learner says only 'platelets help', say: 'Good start. What do they look like, and what does that let them do?'
If the whole class is silent after the wait time, say: 'Think about what is small and has no nucleus. Turn to your partner for 20 seconds.' Then call again.
notes.why_this_works: Calling learners by name means every learner has to be ready to explain. Writing each claim on the timeline makes the chain of cause and effect visible. Common misconception: the cut is healed by one kind of cell doing everything.
answer_key: Question 1: Platelets. They are small, disc-shaped pieces with no nucleus. Their small size lets them travel in the blood and gather at the cut. They are sticky, so they clump and plug it.
Question 2: Platelets are very small and have no nucleus. This leaves small sticky pieces that aggregate (stick together) at the cut and start clotting.
Question 3: Clotting proteins, such as fibrin. Proteins are made on ribosomes, many of which sit on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

slides.title: Stage 4: the immune response
slides.subtitle: Cold-call: one claim each. Everyone else listens.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each of the 2 students

items: Neutrophils arrive. What do they do? Which organelle makes that job possible?
Macrophages: how is their shape different from neutrophils? What can that shape do?

do: Call Student D for question 1 and Student E for question 2.
After each answer, rephrase it and write the key claim at stage 4 on the board.
Tick each learner as called.
say: [Name], neutrophils arrive. What do they do, and what organelle makes that job possible?
[Name], macrophages. How is their shape different from neutrophils? What does that shape allow them to do?
[Name], you said [X]. Can anyone add the organelle or structure detail that makes that work?
look_for: Student D names lysosomes and links them to digesting bacteria.
Student E describes an irregular, flexible shape and links it to engulfing.
Listen to at least 3 uncalled learners nodding or adding. If fewer than 4 learners can name the organelle for a function, pause for a 2-minute review.
if_then: If Student D says only 'they fight germs', say: 'How do they fight them? Which organelle has the digesting enzymes?'
If Student E cannot compare the two, say: 'Picture a cell that can change its shape. What could it wrap around?'
notes.why_this_works: Comparing two similar immune cells makes learners link shape to job rather than memorise names. This answers the unit's driving question one cell at a time.
answer_key: Question 1: Neutrophils engulf bacteria. Lysosomes, full of digesting enzymes, break the bacteria down. They have a multi-lobed nucleus and many lysosomes.
Question 2: Macrophages have an irregular shape and a flexible membrane. This lets them change shape, wrap around and engulf bacteria, debris and dead cells.

slides.title: Stages 5 and 6: rebuild and close
slides.subtitle: Cold-call: one claim each. Everyone else listens.
slides.time_note: About 2 minutes for each of the 2 students

items: Fibroblasts secrete collagen. Which organelle is highly developed? Why is that logical?
Epidermal cells divide and move. Which cell feature must be active for division?

do: Call Student F for question 1 (stage 5) and Student G for question 2 (stage 6).
Write each key claim on the board at the correct stage.
Tick each learner as called.
say: [Name], fibroblasts secrete collagen. What organelle is highly developed in fibroblasts, and why is that logical?
[Name], epidermal cells divide and migrate. What cell feature must be active for division to happen?
[Name], you said [X]. Can anyone add the organelle or structure detail that makes that work?
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after question 1, 10 seconds after question 2.
look_for: Student F links protein-making to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.
Student G names the nucleus (and may add centrioles).
At least 3 uncalled learners are tracking the board.
if_then: If Student F cannot name the organelle, say: 'Collagen is a protein. Which organelle did we say makes and packs proteins?'
If Student G says only 'they split', say: 'What must be copied before a cell can split? Where is it kept?'
notes.why_this_works: Asking 'why is that logical?' moves learners from recall to reasoning: the job decides which organelles the cell needs more of.
answer_key: Question 1: Fibroblasts are elongated and have extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. This is logical because they make and secrete a lot of protein (collagen) to build the scaffold.
Question 2: The nucleus must be active. It holds the DNA, which is copied before the cell divides. Centrioles in animal cells also help division.

slides.title: The hardest question
slides.subtitle: Answer using what you know about specialisation.
slides.time_note: About 3 minutes for the question, 30 seconds of silent reading, then wrap-up

timers.label: Silent reading of the class story

blocks.text: All these cells come from the same organism and carry the same DNA. So why do they look so different?

items: eyes :: Then read the class story on the board in silence
star :: You built this explanation together

do: Call Student H. Choose one of the strongest learners you noted in the Predict phase, because this is the hardest question.
Do not correct a weak answer. Open it to the class.
After the answer, point to the board and give 30 seconds for silent reading of the whole class story.
say: [Name], all these cells come from the same organism and carry the same DNA. So why do they look so different? Answer using what you know about specialisation.
Look at the board. That is the complete answer to the question we started with in Lesson 1. Read it. That explanation belongs to this class. You built it together.
notes.wait_time: 15 seconds after the question. Then 30 seconds of silent reading.
look_for: Student H links DNA, different genes being switched on, and specialisation. At minimum the answer says different genes are 'switched on' in different cells.
Uncalled learners are nodding, tracking the board or raising hands to add.
Check the board: every stage has at least one cell claim written on it.
if_then: If the answer is one clause only, say: 'Who can build on that? Three more words. What is the connection to shape?'
If nobody mentions genes, say: 'The DNA is the same in each cell. So what could be different about how each cell uses it?'
notes.why_this_works: The hardest question comes last, when learners have the evidence of five cell types in front of them. The finished board shows learners their own thinking as a single explanation.
answer_key: Model answer for Student H: 'The cells carry the same DNA, but different genes are switched on in different cells. This gives each cell different structures and organelles. The structure fits the job, so the shape of a cell is not accidental.'

Class story on the board: 1 cut occurs; 2 bleeding begins; 3 platelets (small, no nucleus, sticky) clump and a clot forms; 4 neutrophils (lobed nucleus, many lysosomes) and macrophages (flexible shape) engulf bacteria and debris; 5 fibroblasts (extensive rough ER and Golgi) secrete collagen; 6 epidermal cells divide and migrate to close the skin.

slides.title: Put Lesson 1 beside your final model
slides.subtitle: Look at them side by side.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes to set up and give the instructions

items: book :: Lesson 1 diagram on the left
star :: Your Lesson 11 final model on the right
eyes :: Look at both, side by side

blocks.text: Word wall: organelle, specialisation, cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosome, chloroplast, cell wall, vacuole, lysosome

do: Learners take out their Lesson 1 diagram and their Lesson 11 revised model. Give out the Lesson 11 models if you have kept them.
Write the three sentence stems on the board (they are on the next slide).
Point to the word wall.
say: Put your Lesson 1 diagram on the left and your final model on the right. Look at them side by side.
In 8 minutes, I want you to write three sentences. The stems are on the board.
Use the words from our wall. Be specific. Do not say 'I learned more'. Say what exactly you learned and why the evidence changed your thinking.
look_for: Every learner has both documents side by side before the timer starts. Check the whole room.
if_then: If a learner has no Lesson 11 model, say: 'Use the most recent version of your model, or the group poster, and write about that.'
notes.why_this_works: Putting the two models side by side makes learning growth visible. Learners can point at what changed instead of just saying 'I learned a lot'.

slides.title: Then vs. Now: write three sentences
slides.subtitle: Be specific. Do not write 'I learned more.'

blocks.text: Finish these sentences in your notebook:
items: 1. In Lesson 1, I thought… but now I know… because…
2. The biggest change in my model is… because the evidence from [lesson or activity] showed me…
3. One question I still have is…

do: Write the three stems on the board and keep them visible.
Start the 8-minute timer. Learners write alone and in silence, in their notebooks or on a template.
Circulate and read over shoulders. Read 6–8 responses.
Pick 2 learners with strong, specific answers. Ask them quietly if they are willing to share. Respect a no: reflections are private.
say: Write your three sentences now. Use the words from our wall.
Say exactly what you learned and why the evidence changed your thinking.
notes.wait_time: The full 8 minutes of silent writing.
look_for: Sentences contain specific cell and organelle names, not general statements.
At least one learner names a specific lesson activity as their evidence.
The 'question I still have' sentences show real curiosity, for example how genes are switched on and off or how the body knows which cells to send.
Red flag: most responses are identical or vague. Then stop the class and model one example aloud before they continue.
if_then: If a learner writes only 'I learned more', say: 'Which cell or organelle is new to you? What did you see or do that made you change your mind?'
If most answers are vague, say: 'Stop. Listen to one example.' Then read the model answer for sentence 1 aloud.
If a learner finishes early, say: 'Add the name of the lesson activity that gave you your evidence.'
notes.why_this_works: Sentence stems make learners name the specific evidence behind each change. This moves reflection from vague ('I learned a lot') to precise. Common misconception: 'learning more' is the same as 'changing my model'.
answer_key: Sentence 1: 'In Lesson 1, I thought cells just join together to heal the cut, but now I know different cells do different jobs, because each cell has its own shape and organelles.'
Sentence 2: 'The biggest change in my model is that I added organelles with jobs, because the evidence from the specialised cell lessons showed me that shape fits function.'
Sentence 3: 'One question I still have is how a cell knows which job to do.'

slides.title: Share: what changed in your thinking?
slides.subtitle: Two volunteers share. Then we compare.
slides.time_note: About 4 minutes for sharing and class responses

blocks.text: Who had a similar change in their thinking? Who had a different change?

items: raised_hand :: Show your hand if the change is similar
lightbulb :: A question you still have is not a failure

do: Call on the 2 learners you asked earlier. Let each share one or two sentences.
After each one, ask for hands to show similar changes. Scan the room.
Then ask for hands for a DIFFERENT change. Call on one learner.
Close with the message about the third sentence.
say: [Name], please share what you wrote.
Who else had a similar change in their thinking? Hands.
Who had a DIFFERENT change? Hands.

Your third sentence, the question you still have, is not a failure. That is the beginning of the next unit. Scientists in Kenya and around the world are still asking questions exactly like yours. Hold onto it.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each question before taking hands.
look_for: Count the hands for 'similar' and for 'different'. A good class has at least 8 hands on 'similar' and some on 'different'.
Shared answers name specific cells or organelles.
if_then: If the volunteers give vague answers, say: 'Which cell or organelle changed your thinking? Name it.'
If nobody offers a different change, say: 'Look at your second sentence. Did your evidence come from a different activity? Tell us.'
notes.why_this_works: Hearing classmates' changes shows that learning is built on evidence and revision, and that different learners can be convinced by different evidence.

slides.title: Closing the Driving Question Board
slides.subtitle: Every question card gets a colour.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes to explain how the colours work

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.
ANSWERED :: Green. Strong evidence.
PARTIALLY ANSWERED :: Yellow. Gaps remain.
BEYOND THIS UNIT :: Blue. Needs more biology.

do: Bring the physical Driving Question Board to the front. If it is digital, show it on screen.
Have green, yellow and blue stickers or markers ready.
Prepare a space for the 'Future Questions Wall'.
say: For each question on our board, we decide together.
ANSWERED means we have strong evidence. PARTIALLY ANSWERED means we have some evidence but gaps remain. BEYOND THIS UNIT means this question needs more biology than we have learned so far.
Raise your hand to vote.
look_for: Learners can say in their own words what each colour means. Ask 2 learners to explain one colour each.
if_then: If learners mix up PARTIALLY ANSWERED and BEYOND THIS UNIT, say: 'Partly answered means we have some evidence. Beyond this unit means we have almost none yet.'
notes.why_this_works: A shared rule for classifying questions turns closing the board into an honest check of what the evidence can and cannot tell us.

slides.title: Classify each question card
slides.subtitle: Vote. Give one reason. Mark the card.

items: raised_hand :: Vote with your hand
speech :: Give a one-sentence reason
pushpin :: We mark the card with a colour
arrow_right :: Blue cards go to the Future Questions Wall

do: Work through the board one card at a time. Spend no more than 45 seconds per card.
For ANSWERED cards: cold-call one student for the one-sentence answer.
For PARTIALLY ANSWERED cards: cold-call one student to say what we know and what the gap is.
For BEYOND THIS UNIT cards: ask which future topic might answer it. Take 2–3 hands.
Mark each card: green = ANSWERED, yellow = PARTIALLY ANSWERED, blue = BEYOND THIS UNIT.
Move blue cards to the Future Questions Wall.
say: Who can give the one-sentence answer?
What do we know, and what is the gap?
Which future topic might answer this? Any guesses?

The questions on our future wall are not failures. They are invitations. Some will be answered in later sub-strands, some in other strands, and some you may not meet until university or research. That is what biology looks like: a subject that is still being written.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after asking for a one-sentence answer.
look_for: At least 70% of cards are classified as ANSWERED, each with a correct one-sentence reason.
Reasons use evidence from the class (the class story, the microscope work, the diagrams), not only 'the book says'.
BEYOND THIS UNIT cards make learners curious: they name upcoming topics or ask follow-up questions.
if_then: If a class vote seems wrong, say: 'What evidence do we have for that? Who can point to it?'
If a card is unclear, say: 'Does this question ask about cell structure, or about something we have not studied yet?'
If time runs short, say: 'We will do the last cards by vote only, with no reasons.'
notes.why_this_works: A public vote with a one-sentence reason makes learners judge their own evidence. Common misconception: an unanswered question means the unit failed. The Future Questions Wall shows that it means the science goes on.

slides.title: Can we answer the driving question now?
slides.subtitle: One full sentence. Use cell structure and specialisation.

blocks.text: Why do cells in our body look so different from each other, and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?

items: microscope :: Use cell structure
puzzle :: Use specialisation
bandage :: Name at least two cell types

do: Point to the driving question that has been on the board since Lesson 1.
Cold-call one learner for a final, full-sentence answer. Choose a learner who gave a good claim earlier in the round.
say: Can we answer this now?
[Name], give me your best final answer in full sentences.
look_for: The answer is full and accurate, and covers cell structure, specialisation and at least two named cell types.
Listen to how many learners nod or add. Ask 2 more learners to add one extra detail.
if_then: If the answer is one word or one clause, do not correct. Say: 'Who can build on that? Three more words. What is the connection to shape?'
If a learner gives only a definition, say: 'Now link it to a cell from the cut finger. Which one?'
notes.why_this_works: Asking for a full-sentence answer to the very first question shows learners how far they have come. Common misconception: shape is only for show.
answer_key: Model answer: 'Cells in our body look different because they are specialised. Different genes are switched on, so each cell has different structures and organelles. Shape fits the job: platelets are small and sticky to plug a cut, neutrophils have many lysosomes to digest bacteria, and fibroblasts have lots of rough ER to make collagen.'

slides.title: Exit reflection
slides.subtitle: This is about your own thinking, not a grade.

blocks.text: One thing I now understand that I did not understand in Lesson 1 is… because…

items: The evidence that changed my thinking was…
Use the language of cell biology.

do: Learners write alone in their notebooks.
Collect the exit reflections at the end. They help you plan the next sub-strand.
Remind learners that personal reflections are private and will not be read aloud without consent.
say: Before we close, I want one last piece of individual writing from you. This is for you. It is about your own thinking, not a grade.
Complete this sentence in your notebook: One thing I now understand that I did not understand in Lesson 1 is… because… The evidence that changed my thinking was…
You have 5 minutes. Be specific. Use the language of cell biology.
look_for: Read at least 8 reflections while learners write.
Strong: each names a specific cell type, organelle or evidence activity.
Red flag: generic statements such as 'I learned a lot about cells'.
if_then: If a learner is stuck, say: 'Pick one cell from the cut finger. What did you not know about it in Lesson 1?'
If a learner writes a generic statement, say: 'Which activity showed you this? Add its name.'
notes.why_this_works: The exit reflection is each learner's own final statement of their model, with the evidence behind it. Collecting it gives you data for the next sub-strand.
answer_key: Model answer: 'One thing I now understand that I did not understand in Lesson 1 is that cells in the same body have different shapes because each is specialised for a job. The evidence that changed my thinking was the class story, where platelets, neutrophils and fibroblasts each had a shape and organelles that fitted their job.'

slides.title: Get ready for the assessment
slides.subtitle: Clear your desks. Work alone and in silence.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes to settle and give out the papers

items: door :: Clear your desks
hand :: Work alone
hourglass :: Work in silence
star :: Show how far you have come

do: Check that no scissors or sharp objects are on desks.
Give out the assessment papers and check each learner has one.
Tell learners where the word wall or vocabulary sheet is, if school policy allows them to use it.
say: Well done. You have worked hard across twelve lessons.
The assessment you are about to do is an opportunity to show what you know. It is not a test of whether you are clever. It is a record of how far you have come.
Clear your desks. Work independently and in silence. You have the time set by our school policy.
look_for: Every desk is clear and every learner has a paper. Scan the whole room.
if_then: If a learner asks a content question, say: 'I cannot answer content questions now. Do your best.'
If a learner is stuck, point to the word wall or vocabulary sheet, if school policy permits.
notes.why_this_works: A calm, clear routine and a kind framing reduce test anxiety and help learners show what they really know.

slides.title: Sub-strand assessment
slides.subtitle: Work alone. Show what you know.
slides.time_note: The teacher sets the time as per school policy; 15 minutes is used here to fit the 80-minute lesson

items: microscope :: Label and describe a specialised cell
maize :: Explain structure and function in a Kenyan context
leaf :: Compare plant and animal cells
bandage :: Questions on wound healing and specialisation

do: Learners sit the sub-strand summative assessment independently and in silence.
Circulate silently. Do not answer content questions.
Collect papers at the end.
Close with the final message below. Then mark by SLO (see LOOK FOR).
say: In Lesson 1, you saw a cut finger and guessed. Today, you can explain it cell by cell. That is what learning biology looks like. Take that with you into the next sub-strand.
notes.wait_time: Silent for the full assessment time.
look_for: Learners write continuously without asking a neighbour for help.
In the wound healing question, learners sequence at least 3 correct cell types in the correct order with accurate structural details. Check at least 5 scripts as you collect them.
When marking, analyse results by SLO: cell structure labelling, specialisation explanation, plant vs. animal comparison. Note the strongest and weakest SLOs.
if_then: If a learner appears stuck, point to the word wall or the vocabulary sheet (if school policy permits). Do not give hints.
If a learner is finished early, say: 'Read your answers again. Check that you named the cell and one structure for each answer.'
notes.why_this_works: Doing the assessment right after the exit reflection lets learners use the thinking they have just written down. The results show which outcomes were secure and which to revisit.
answer_key: The assessment paper and marking scheme are not given in the lesson plan. Mark with the school's own scheme.

Model wound-healing sequence for the long question: platelets (small, no nucleus, sticky) clump and start the clot; neutrophils (lobed nucleus, many lysosomes) engulf bacteria; macrophages (flexible shape) engulf debris and dead cells; fibroblasts (extensive rough ER and Golgi) secrete collagen; epidermal cells (active nucleus) divide and move to close the skin.

lesson_oneliner: Explain the healing cut cell by cell, then close our Driving Question Board.
purpose: Students return to the healing cut for the last time. They use eleven lessons of evidence to explain it cell by cell.
They compare their Lesson 1 thinking with their final model and name what changed and why.
The class closes the Driving Question Board honestly: answered, partly answered, or beyond this unit.
Students write an exit reflection and sit the sub-strand assessment. This shows how far they have come.
before_class: Every learner can find their Lesson 1 diagram and written prediction (teacher files or portfolios).
Every learner has their Lesson 11 revised model, or the group poster if that is all they have.
Write the phenomenon on the board in full before learners come in.
Have the full Driving Question Board ready at the front, with every question card posted since Lesson 1.
Have green, yellow and blue stickers or markers ready, plus space for a Future Questions Wall.
Prepare the word wall: organelle, specialisation, cell membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosome, chloroplast, cell wall, vacuole, lysosome.
Print the sub-strand assessment papers. Clear scissors and sharp objects from the desks.
Choose your 8 cold-call learners by name before the Observe phase.
do_not_show: Do not show the cold-call question slides until learners have finished their silent writing in the Predict phase.
Do not write the finished class story on the board before the cold-call round. It is built by learners, stage by stage.
Do not show the slide 'Can we answer the driving question now?' until every question card is classified.

summary.observe_prompt: Which cells did the class name, and how many students spoke?
summary.learn_prompt: Why do cells from one body look so different?
summary.explain_prompt: Explain the healing cut, cell by cell.
summary.next_lesson: New questions from our Future Questions Wall.
summary.answer_observe: The class built a complete, sequenced, cell-by-cell explanation of wound healing on the board, from the cut to closed skin. We named platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts and epidermal cells, with their shapes and key organelles. At least 8 students contributed by cold-call.
summary.answer_learn: All specialised cells in the body come from the same organism and carry the same DNA. Different genes are expressed in different cells, so they make different structures. Those structures decide the function. The shape of a cell is not accidental: it shows the job the cell is specialised to do.
summary.answer_explain: Platelets (small, no nucleus, sticky) clump and start the clot. Neutrophils (multi-lobed nucleus, many lysosomes) engulf bacteria. Macrophages (irregular, flexible membrane) engulf debris and dead cells. Fibroblasts (elongated, extensive rough ER and Golgi) secrete collagen. Epidermal cells (tightly packed, active nucleus) divide and migrate to close the skin. Each shape solves one job, so cells in one body look different.
reflection: Which learning outcome grew most from Lesson 1 to Lesson 12, and which teaching moves caused that growth?

How many learners could explain wound healing with 3 or more named cell types and accurate structural details?
Did the exit reflections name specific activities as evidence, or only general statements? What does that say about how evidence was recorded?
Which Driving Question Board questions were marked BEYOND THIS UNIT? How can they lead into the next sub-strand?
